evidence.claim: A 183-foot Doric column rises from a Corinthian portico at the Louisville Water Tower.
evidence.quote: The main column, of the Doric order, rises 183 feet (55.8 m) out of a Corinthian portico surrounding its base.

evidence.claim: Theodore Scowden and Charles Hermany designed the structures as an ornament intended to win over residents skeptical of the water company.
evidence.quote: It was decided to render the water station an ornament to the city, to make skeptical Louisvillians more accepting of a water company. Theodore Scowden and his assistant Charles Hermany were the architects of the structures.

evidence.claim: Pumping began in 1860 and ended here in 1909.
evidence.quote: The water tower began operations on October 16, 1860.

evidence.claim: Pumping began in 1860 and ended here in 1909.
evidence.quote: the original water tower ceased pumping operations in 1909.

evidence.claim: The column has changed since its first working days: an 1890 tornado destroyed the wood-paneled shaft that protected its iron pipe, and cast iron replaced it.
evidence.quote: A tornado on March 27, 1890 irreparably changed the Water Tower. The original water tower had an iron pipe protected by a wood-paneled shaft, but after the tornado destroyed it, it was replaced with cast iron.

evidence.claim: The riverside location served the machinery as well as the architecture: coal boats could deliver the fuel needed to operate the station.
evidence.quote: The location also meant that coal boats could easily deliver the coal necessary to operate the station.

evidence.claim: The Doric column rises above a Corinthian portico.

evidence.claim: Its name began with a horse farm: James C. McFerran bought the estate in 1868 and called his farm Glen View.
evidence.quote: The estate was purchased in 1868 by meat packer James C. McFerran. McFerran's horse farm was named "Glen View".

evidence.claim: After McFerran’s death in 1885, John E. Green acquired it and renamed it Glenview Stock Farm.
evidence.quote: After his death in 1885, John E. Green acquired the farm and renamed it "Glenview Stock Farm".
